summary: Describes measures to make DNS resolvers much harder to fool with forged answers, such as behavior that had not previously been standardized. It addresses a serious threat while DNS security was not yet fully deployed. This is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2181.

plainLanguage.summary: A DNS resolver looks up a name by sending a question and accepting the first answer that comes back and looks right. This RFC says exactly which parts of the question the answer has to match, and asks resolvers to randomise the port and the identifier they use, so that a forger on the network has to make far more guesses.

questions: how hard is it to forge a dns answer
what must a dns resolver check in a response
subtitle: Making a DNS resolver much harder to trick with a made-up answer.

tldr.problem: A resolver accepts the first answer that matches its outstanding query, and there are only a few things a resolver can check, so a third party on the network can often get a fake answer accepted first.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out rules for what a resolver must match before accepting an answer, and requires it to use an unpredictable source port, an unpredictable query ID and, where it can, an unpredictable source address.
tldr.outcome: The number of guesses an attacker has to make grows by a factor of about 64000, which puts the attack out of reach of ordinary bandwidth.

facts.label: Packets needed on a first attempt
Bandwidth needed with an unknown port

today: RFC 5452 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2181. It has not itself been obsoleted or updated, and it describes measures that make the existing DNS more resilient until a cryptographically enhanced protocol is deployed.

sections.title: Why the Document Exists
sections.content:
The document describes several common problems in DNS implementations which, although previously recognised, remain largely unsolved. Besides briefly recapping these problems, it contains rules that, if implemented, make complying resolvers vastly more resistant to the attacks described. The goal is to make the existing DNS as secure as possible within the current protocol boundaries.

The words are aimed at authors of resolvers. It is up to operators to decide which nameserver implementation to use and which options to enable, and operational constraints may override the security concerns described. Implementations are expected to allow an operator to enable the functionality described in the document.

Almost every transaction on the Internet involves the Domain Name System. It has also recently become possible to acquire SSL and TLS certificates with no confirmation of identity beyond the ability to answer a verification email sent by SMTP, which generally uses DNS for its routing. Any party that temporarily controls the Domain Name System is therefore in a position to reroute most kinds of Internet transaction, including the verification steps in acquiring such a certificate, which means that even transactions protected by SSL and TLS could be diverted.

These developments have made the security and trustworthiness of DNS of renewed importance. Although the DNS community is working hard on finalising and implementing a cryptographically enhanced DNS protocol, steps should be taken to make sure that the existing use of DNS is as secure as possible within the bounds of the relevant standards. The document notes that the most commonly used resolvers at the time did not perform as well as possible in this respect, which makes it of urgent importance.

It also notes that even when all the measures suggested are implemented, protocol users are not protected against third parties who can observe, modify or inject packets in the traffic of a resolver. For protocol extensions that offer protection against those scenarios, the document points to RFC 4033 and beyond.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost everything on the Internet starts with a name lookup, and even an encrypted connection depends on that lookup being right. The document does not change the DNS protocol; it tells resolver authors how to make the resolver they already wrote much harder to fool.

sections.title: The Words the Document Uses
sections.content:
A client is typically a stub resolver on an end user's computer. A resolver is a nameserver performing recursive service for clients, also known as a caching server or a full service resolver. A stub resolver is a very limited resolver on a client computer that leaves the recursing work to a full resolver.

A query is a question sent out by a resolver, typically in a UDP packet, and a response is the answer sent back by an authoritative nameserver, typically in a UDP packet. A third party is any entity other than the resolver or the intended recipient of a question; it may have access to an arbitrary authoritative nameserver but has no access to the packets transmitted by the resolver or the authoritative server. An attacker is a malicious third party, and spoofing is the activity of attempting to subvert the DNS process by getting a chosen answer accepted.

An authentic response is the correct answer from the right authoritative server. The target domain name is the domain the attacker wishes to spoof in an answer, and the fake data is the response chosen by the attacker.
sections.plainLanguage: The words to tell apart are the resolver, which does the work of looking names up, and the third party, which has no access to the traffic but can still send packets. Spoofing means getting a made-up answer accepted as if it were the real one.

sections.title: How a Resolver Is Fooled
sections.content:
When certain steps are taken, it is feasible to spoof the deployed majority of resolvers with carefully crafted and timed DNS packets. Once spoofed, a caching server repeats the data it wrongfully accepted and makes its clients contact the wrong, and possibly malicious, servers.

To understand the process, it is important to know what makes a resolver accept a response. A sentence in Section 5.3.3 of RFC 1034 presaged the problem: the resolver should be highly paranoid in its parsing of responses, and should check that the response matches the query it sent using the ID field in the response.

DNS data is to be accepted by a resolver if and only if four conditions hold. The question section of the reply packet must be equivalent to that of a question packet currently waiting for a response. The ID field of the reply must match that of the question packet. The response must come from the same network address to which the question was sent. And the response must come in on the same network address, including port number, from which the question was sent. In general, the first response matching these four conditions is accepted.

If a third party succeeds in meeting the four conditions before the response from the authentic nameserver does, it is in a position to feed the resolver fabricated data. When it does so, the document calls it an attacker attempting to spoof in fake data. All the conditions can theoretically be met by a third party, with the difficulty being a function of the resolver implementation and the zone configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver accepts an answer when four things line up: the question is one it is still waiting for, the identifier matches, and the answer came from the address and the port the question was sent to and from. The first answer that lines up wins, so the forger has to be first.

sections.title: How Much Work Each Condition Is
sections.content:
Forcing a query. Formally there is no need for a nameserver to perform service except for its operator, its customers or more generally its users, but open recursing nameservers have been used to amplify denial-of-service attacks. Providing full service enables a third party to send the target resolver a query for the domain name it intends to spoof. On receiving that query, and not finding the answer in its cache, the resolver transmits queries to the relevant authoritative nameservers, which opens a window of opportunity. Queries may also be forced indirectly, for example by inducing a mail server to perform DNS lookups. Some operators restrict access by not recursing for unauthorised addresses but only answering from the cache, which makes spoofing harder because the third party can no longer force the exact moment a question is asked. It is still possible to determine a time range, because nameservers publish the decreasing time to live of their cached entries, which indicate from which absolute time a new query could be sent. The time to live of the target domain's record sets therefore determines how often a window of opportunity is available, and a short time to live makes spoofing far more viable.

The question section and the ID field. Both queries and responses contain a question section, and incoming responses should be verified to have a question section equivalent to that of the outgoing query. The DNS ID field is 16 bits wide, so with full use of all those bits and truly random contents it takes on average 32768 attempts to guess. Anecdotal evidence suggests there are implementations using only 14 bits, which means 8192 attempts on average will do. If the target nameserver can be forced into having several identical queries outstanding, the birthday attack phenomenon means that any fake data is matched against several outstanding queries, which raises the chance of success considerably.

The source address. Meeting this condition means being able to transmit packets on behalf of the address of the authoritative nameserver. Two Best Current Practice documents direct Internet access providers to prevent their customers from assuming addresses that are not assigned to them, but these recommendations are not universally, or even widely, implemented. Many zones have two or three authoritative nameservers, which makes matching the source address of the authentic response very likely even with a naive choice, and most recursing nameservers store performance indications that make it easier to predict which nameserver would be queried first. Generally this condition takes at most two or three attempts.

The destination address and port. The destination address of the authentic response is the source address of the original query. The address of a recursing nameserver is generally known, but the port used for asking questions is harder to determine: most current resolvers pick an arbitrary port at startup, possibly at random, and use it for all outgoing queries, and in quite a number of cases the source port is fixed at the traditional DNS server port number of 53. If the source port of the original query is random but static, any authoritative nameserver under observation can reveal it, so matching this condition often requires no guesswork. If multiple ports are used, the effective identifier space grows by a factor equal to the number of ports used. Less common resolvers choose a random port for every outgoing query, in which case the port is an additional identifier field of up to 16 bits. If the maximum port range is used, around 32256 source ports have to be tried on average before the right one is found, as ports below 1024 may be unavailable, leaving 64512 options. It is generally safe for DNS to use ports in the range 1024 to 49152, even though some of those ports are allocated to other protocols, and a resolver that uses a port should release it after a short time and move to a different one. A firewall will not prevent the matching of this address, since it accepts answers that appear to come from the correct address.

The timing. Once a packet has matched the previous four conditions, no further responses are generally accepted, so the third party has a limited time in which to inject its spoofed response. For calculations the document assumes a window of at most 100 milliseconds, depending on the network distance to the authentic authoritative nameserver, and notes that the period can be far longer if the authentic nameservers are briefly overloaded by queries, perhaps by the attacker.
sections.plainLanguage: The hardest part for a forger is guessing the identifier and matching the port and address. The identifier is only sixteen bits, and some resolvers use even fewer. The address is usually easy because a zone has two or three servers. The port is the interesting one: many resolvers always use port 53, and an attacker who watches the traffic can learn the port even when it is random but fixed.

sections.title: Birthday Attacks and In-Domain Records
sections.content:
The birthday paradox implies that a group of 23 people suffices to have a more than even chance of two or more of them sharing a birthday. An attacker benefits from the same phenomenon if it can force the target resolver to have several equivalent outstanding queries, identical in name, type and class, at any one time to the same authoritative server. Any packet the attacker then sends has a much higher chance of being accepted, because it only has to match any one of the outstanding queries for that single domain. As long as small numbers of queries are sent out, the chance of successfully spoofing a response rises linearly with the number of outstanding queries for the exact domain and nameserver; for larger numbers the effect is less pronounced.

A second rule concerns what may be accepted at all. Responses from authoritative nameservers often contain information that is not part of the zone for which the resolver treats them as authoritative: a query for the mail exchanger record of a domain might get a mail exchanger in another domain, and additionally the IP address of that mail exchanger. If accepted uncritically, the resolver stands the chance of accepting data from an untrusted source. Care must be taken to accept data only if it is known that the originator is authoritative for the name that was asked for, or for a parent of it. One very simple way to achieve this is to accept data only if it is part of the domain the query was intended for.
sections.plainLanguage: Two further rules help. If a resolver has several identical questions outstanding at once, a single fake answer has many chances to match one of them, so a forger who can force that situation gets a much better deal. And a resolver should not take data about names outside the domain it asked about, because that data can come from anywhere.

sections.title: What the Attack Costs the Attacker
sections.content:
With a known or static destination port, matching the identifier field and the source and destination addresses takes on average in the order of 2 times 2 to the power of 15, which is about 65000 packets, assuming a zone has two authoritative nameservers. If the window of opportunity is around 100 milliseconds, an attacker would need to be able to briefly transmit 650000 packets per second to have a 50% chance of getting spoofed data accepted on the first attempt. A realistic minimal DNS response consists of around 80 bytes including IP headers, which makes that packet rate a burst of 416 Mbit/s. At the time of writing, that kind of bandwidth was not common but not scarce either, especially for those in a position to control many servers.

These numbers change when a window of a full second is assumed, possibly because the arrival of the authentic response is prevented by overloading the real authoritative hosts with decoy queries, which reduces the needed bandwidth to 42 Mbit/s. If the attacker is granted more than a single chance and allowed up to 60 minutes of work on a domain with a time to live of 300 seconds, a meager 4 Mbit/s suffices for a 50% chance of getting fake data accepted.

The calculation uses these symbols: I is the number of distinct identifiers available, at most 65536; P is the number of ports used, at most around 64000, though ports below 1024 are not always available and are often just one; N is the number of authoritative nameservers for a domain, averaging around 2.5; F is the number of fake packets sent; R is the number of packets sent per second; W is the window of opportunity in seconds, bounded by the response time of the authoritative servers and often 0.1; D is the average number of identical outstanding queries of a resolver, typically one; and A is the number of attempts, one for each window of opportunity. The probability of being spoofed is the amount of fake packets arriving within the window divided by the size of the problem space, and with common values it reduces to a simple expression in the packet rate. The combined chance over a chosen period is worked out from the fact that a new window opens each time the time to live expires.

From this the document concludes that if the nameserver implementation is unchanged, only raising the time to live offers protection, because raising the number of authoritative nameservers is not feasible beyond a small number. It also notes an important assumption in the calculations: a known or static destination port. If that port is unknown and has to be guessed as well, the problem space expands by a factor of 64000, leading the attacker to need in excess of 285 Gb/s to achieve similar success rates. Such bandwidth is not generally available, nor expected to be in the foreseeable future. Some firewalls may need reconfiguring if they are set up to allow outgoing queries from a single DNS source port.

Techniques are available to use an effectively unlimited number of queries, which reduces the effective time to live to zero. With the same rate of 7000 packets per second and one source port, the spoofing chance rises to 50% within 7 seconds. If 64000 ports are used, as the document recommends, the same query rate reaches the 50% level after around 116 hours. The document also notes that the attacks can be detected by watchful server operators, since an unexpected incoming stream of 4.5 Mbit/s of packets might be noticed.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does the arithmetic for the attacker. With a fixed, known port, a forger needs a burst of hundreds of megabits a second to win a first attempt. If the port is unknown as well, the burst has to be hundreds of gigabits a second, which nobody has. Randomising the port is therefore what turns a feasible attack into an impractical one.

sections.title: The Countermeasures
sections.content:
A resolver implementation must match responses to all of the following attributes of the query before applying the DNS trustworthiness rules: source address against query destination address, destination address against query source address, destination port against query source port, query ID, query name, and query class and type. A mismatch means the response must be considered invalid.

Resolver implementations must use an unpredictable source port for outgoing queries, from the range of available ports, 53 or 1024 and above, as large as possible and practicable; use multiple different source ports at the same time in case of multiple outstanding queries; and use an unpredictable query ID for outgoing queries, using the full range available from 0 to 65535. Resolvers with several IP addresses should use them in an unpredictable manner for outgoing queries, and should provide means to avoid the use of certain ports. Resolvers should favour authoritative nameservers with which a trust relation has been established, and stub resolvers should be able to use Transaction Signatures or IPsec when talking to their recursive resolver. Where a cryptographic verification of response validity is available, a resolver may waive the rules above and rely on that guarantee instead. Proper unpredictability requires a high quality pseudo-random generator.

The justification is that an attacker can force a full resolver to send queries to the attacker's own nameservers, so any constant or sequential state held by the resolver can be measured and must not be trivially easy to reverse engineer in a way that predicts future state. A full resolver with only one or a small number of upstream-facing endpoints is effectively using constants for the source address and the UDP port, and those are very predictable. A resolver that uses a simple increment to get its next query ID is likewise very predictable and very spoofable. Weak random number generators have been shown to expose their internal state, so that an attacker who witnesses several sequential random values can predict the next ones.

If a resolver detects that an attempt is being made to spoof it, perhaps by discovering that many packets fail the criteria above, it may abandon the UDP query and re-issue it over TCP, which by its use of sequence numbers is far more resilient against forgery by third parties.

The security considerations say that the recommendations are complementary to a cryptographically enhanced DNS, which protects against a larger class of attacks, and that a resolver that does not implement them can easily be forced to accept spoofed responses, which are then passed on to client computers and misdirect traffic to possibly malicious entities. The effects of source port randomisation may be dramatically reduced by NAT devices that either serialise or limit in volume the UDP source ports used by the querying resolver. Recursive servers behind a NAT or a stateful firewall may consume all available translation entries under high query load, and port randomisation consumes them faster than a fixed query port would. To avoid that, such devices can and should purge outgoing DNS query translation entries 10 to 17 seconds after the last outgoing query on that mapping was sent, and devices compliant with RFC 4787 need to treat UDP messages with port 53 differently from most other UDP protocols. To minimise the potential that port and state exhaustion attacks can be staged from the outside, it is recommended that services generating a number of DNS queries for each connection should be rate limited, in particular email servers.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules come down to three things: check every part of the answer against the question, use a random port and a random identifier for each question, and if you notice packets failing the checks, repeat the question over TCP. The document also warns that network address translation can undo the port randomisation, so the equipment doing that translation has to keep up.

viz.caption: THE FOUR CONDITIONS A RESOLVER CHECKS

items.title: The question section
items.text: The reply's question section must match a question that is still waiting for an answer.

items.title: The ID field
items.text: The reply's ID must match the ID of the question packet.

items.title: The source address
items.text: The reply must come from the address the question was sent to.

items.title: The source port
items.text: The reply must arrive on the address and port the question was sent from.

cells: Widens the space the attacker has to search
Uses a different port for each outstanding query
Uses the whole range from 0 to 65535
Uses the resolver's several addresses unpredictably
Rejects any answer that differs in address, port, ID, name, class or type

viz.caption: THE SPOOFING PROBABILITY FORMULAS FROM RFC 5452

data.title: Probability of a successful spoof
data.code:
P_s  = (D * F) / (N * P * I)
F    = R * W
P_cs = 1 - (1 - P_s) ^ (T / TTL)

I  identifiers available     P  ports used
N  authoritative nameservers D  identical queries outstanding
R  packets per second        W  window of opportunity in seconds

cells: 60 minutes on a domain with a 300 second TTL
